title: Meter and Time Signatures
intro: Meter is the regular grouping of beats into bars (measures), with the first beat of each bar the strongest. The time signature names the meter: how many beats per bar and which note value gets the beat, or how each beat divides.

blocks.text: Reading a time signature

In simple meters the top number is the number of beats per bar and the bottom number is the note value of one beat (4 = quarter, 2 = half, 8 = eighth). 3/4 is three quarter-note beats per bar; 2/2 ('cut time') is two half-note beats.
Simple and compound meter

In a simple meter each beat divides into two: a quarter-note beat into two eighths. In a compound meter each beat divides into three, so the beat is a dotted note. 6/8 has two dotted-quarter beats, each made of three eighths; 9/8 has three such beats and 12/8 four.

items: Duple: two beats per bar. Simple duple 2/4 or 2/2 (marches); compound duple 6/8 (jigs, many ballads).
Triple: three beats per bar. Simple triple 3/4 (waltzes, minuets); compound triple 9/8.
Quadruple: four beats per bar. Simple quadruple 4/4, also written C ('common time'), the most common meter in Western popular music; compound quadruple 12/8 (slow blues, doo-wop ballads).

blocks.text: 6/8 and 3/4 both hold six eighth notes, but they feel different. 3/4 is three beats of two eighths (ONE-and TWO-and THREE-and); 6/8 is two beats of three (ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six). Beaming shows which: in 6/8 eighths are beamed in threes, in 3/4 in twos.
(The widget plays all notes at one loudness, so the pattern is shown by pitch: the high note marks each beat.)
Strong and weak beats

Meter is a hierarchy of accents. In 4/4 beat 1 is strongest, beat 3 next, beats 2 and 4 weakest; in 3/4 beat 1 is strong and 2 and 3 weak. Harmony tends to change on strong beats, and a dissonance placed on a strong beat sounds more pointed than one on a weak beat. Rock and soul reverse the surface accent with a backbeat on 2 and 4 (the snare drum), while the underlying meter stays the same.
Asymmetric and changing meters

Meters with 5 or 7 beats group them unevenly: 5/8 as 3 + 2 or 2 + 3, 7/8 as 2 + 2 + 3 and so on. These are common in Balkan folk music and in progressive rock and jazz ('Take Five' is in 5/4, grouped 3 + 2). Some pieces change meter from bar to bar, as in Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring.
Beaming

Beams group notes to show the beat. In 4/4, eighths are beamed in twos or fours but never across the middle of the bar (between beats 2 and 3), so the reader can see where beat 3 falls. In compound meters they are beamed in threes. Good beaming is as much a part of notation as correct pitches; Gould's Behind Bars sets out the conventions.
Anacrusis

A melody that starts before the first strong beat begins with an anacrusis (pickup). 'Happy Birthday' starts on a pickup of a dotted eighth and a sixteenth ('Hap-py') before the downbeat ('BIRTH-day'). The final bar is usually shortened to balance the pickup.
At the piano

Count aloud while you play: '1 and 2 and' for simple meters, '1 la li 2 la li' for compound. Practise each hand alone against a metronome set to the beat, then to the subdivision. Waltz accompaniment is a classic exercise in 3/4: bass note on beat 1, a chord in the right range on beats 2 and 3.

widget.title: Waltz accompaniment: bass on 1, chord on 2 and 3 (C, G7, C)

blocks.text: Play along at the piano

items: Step 1. Set a metronome (or the tempo slider) to 80. Play middle C on every click, counting '1 2 3 4' aloud.
Step 2. Now play C on 1 and 3 only (half notes), then on every half-click (eighth notes: '1 and 2 and').
Step 3. Waltz: left hand C3 on beat 1, right hand G3–C4–E4 on beats 2 and 3. Count '1 2 3'.
Step 4. 6/8: play six quick notes per bar with the accent on 1 and 4: 'ONE two three FOUR five six'.
Step 5. Step through the waltz example above to check where each chord falls.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Classify
blocks.text: Classify each meter as simple or compound and duple, triple or quadruple: 3/8, 12/8, 2/2, 9/4.
solution: 3/8: simple triple (three eighth-note beats). 12/8: compound quadruple (four dotted-quarter beats). 2/2: simple duple (two half-note beats). 9/4: compound triple (three dotted-half beats).
blocks.answer: 3/8 simple triple; 12/8 compound quadruple; 2/2 simple duple; 9/4 compound triple

blocks.title: Fill the bar
blocks.text: A bar of 6/8 contains a dotted quarter and an eighth note. What single note value completes it?
solution: 6/8 holds six eighths. A dotted quarter is three eighths and the eighth is one: four used, two left. Two eighths make a quarter note.
